newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Hun Sen's forces face barrier of countless mines.
newsitem.headline: Hun Sen's forces face barrier of countless mines.

text.p: Cambodian forces under Hun Sen are determined to capture the last town held by troops loyal to ousted Prince Norodom Ranariddh but they must first safely navigate through a hidden carpet of landmines before launching a final attack.

The road northeast of the town of Samrong, up to the royalist-held O'Smach on the border with Thailand, is pockmarked with small holes where mines have been cleared, but many more remain just beneath the red-dirt surface and hidden in nearby undergrowth.
A pair of bloody army trousers, a single shoe and a large patch of dried blood lay next to a small crater in the track where one luckless soldier stepped on a mine. He later died, his comrades said.
"Now they are in their last important base, they cannot retreat any more. This is the first time we're facing strong resistance," field commander Chan Cha told Reuters on Sunday.
"If we attack we're going to step on their mine field, this is the main problem, this is a very difficult situation," he said.
Second Prime Minster Hun Sen ousted his senior co-premier Ranariddh on July 6 after two days of battles in Phnom Penh.
Fighting broke out soon after between royalist forces and government troops under Hun Sen in northwest Cambodia. Ranariddh's men withdrew to O'Smach in the north, blowing up bridges as they went.
The front line was active on Sunday with government artillery occasionally firing at royalist positions 15 km (10 miles) or so away.

Every now and then a heavy machine-gun stuttered, breaking the silence of the remote bush, but there was no small arms fire and government commanders said it would be at least a few days before they were ready to attack.
Small villages in the area were deserted, their inhabitants having fled toward the border with Thailand or deeper into government-held territory.

Chan Cha, walking carefully down a path in the gravel road, pointed into the bush just at the side where a barely discernible trip-wire led to a round home-made mine about the size of a large coffee tin.
"Pol Pot mine," said a soldier, referring to the former commander of the Khmer Rouge guerrilla group.
Further up the track, soldiers unearthed two small pieces of wood, rigged together and wired to a battery and another mine.
When stepped on, the pieces of wood are pushed together, completing an electrical circuit triggering the nearby bomb.
"Now the most difficult thing is that the Khmer Rouge cooperate with FUNCINPEC to lay mines in the road," Chan Cha said.

The Khmer Rouge, responsible for the deaths of at least a million people during their 1975-79 rule, are still fighting Hun Sen's government and have called for an alliance between all parties opposed to him.

Ranariddh formed a political alliance with guerrilla front man Khieu Samphan just before the prince's ouster but royalist officials say they are not cooperating militarily with the notorious rebel group.
